facts.text: Galen, a Greek physician born in AD 129, believed that venous blood was made in the liver and sent out to the body, where it was used up.
In the Galenic tradition, the liver turned food into blood, and the organs absorbed this blood as nourishment.
Galen’s ideas had been taught and respected for a very long time, and people still followed them in Harvey’s day.
William Harvey was born on 1 April 1578, studied at Cambridge and then at Padua, where his teacher Fabricius had discovered the valves in veins.
Harvey died on 3 June 1657.
In 1628 Harvey published his book on the motion of the heart and blood, De motu cordis, in Frankfurt; the first edition was a short book of 72 pages.
In the book, Harvey assumed that the left ventricle of the heart holds about two ounces of blood; in a dead body he had found it held a little over two ounces.
He supposed that each beat pushes out only part of this, perhaps a quarter, or as little as an eighth.
Harvey noted that the heart beats more than 1,000 times in half an hour, and in some people two, three or even four thousand times.
Even with these small amounts, he argued, more blood would pass from the heart into the arteries in half an hour than the whole body contains.
For a sheep, he estimated that about three and a half pounds of blood would leave the heart in half an hour, yet he had found that a sheep’s body holds no more than about four pounds of blood.
Harvey said that even if this amount took an hour or a whole day rather than half an hour to pass through the heart, more blood would still flow than food could supply or the veins could hold.
From his figures he concluded that the liver could not make enough new blood from daily food, so the same blood must keep moving around the body in a circle.
Harvey tied a band tightly around a person’s upper arm, which made the veins in the forearm swell and showed the valves inside them.
When he tried to push blood in a vein down the forearm toward the hand it would not move, but pushed up the arm toward the heart it moved easily.
This showed that blood in the veins flows toward the heart and that the valves keep the flow going one way.
Harvey studied cold-blooded animals such as frogs, whose blood moves more slowly, so he could see the blood being pumped more clearly.
Harvey’s use of measurements and calculations of blood volume has been described as the first application of measurement to the study of living things.
Harvey’s theory was not accepted at first; it led to public attacks and a decline in his medical practice, but it had gained recognition by the time he died.
Using a microscope on the lungs of a living frog, Marcello Malpighi described the capillaries that link the arteries with the veins; his letters about this were first printed in 1661.
Malpighi’s capillaries showed how blood gets from the arteries to the veins, completing Harvey’s proof and settling the last real argument against it.
Malpighi’s capillary findings appeared in 1661, four years after Harvey’s death in 1657.
